# Undoing changes {#sec-undoing-changes}

When working with Git, you will inevitably make mistakes or changes that you later want to undo. For example, you might accidentally stage a file, make unwanted changes to a file, or discover an error in a commit.

Git provides several commands for undoing changes, depending on whether the changes are in the working tree, the staging area, or have already been committed. Some commands allow you to undo changes while preserving your work, whereas others permanently discard changes.

In this chapter, you will learn how to use `git commit --amend` to modify the most recent commit, `git restore` to unstage or discard changes, and `git reset` to undo commits. You will also learn when to use each command and how to avoid accidentally losing your work.

## Amending the current commit

A common mistake is to make an error in the commit log message, or making a premature commit where you forgot to stage all the intended changes. You could fix the mistake by making another commit where you staged the forgotten changes or updated the commit message, but there is a more elegant way to fix these types of issues. You can simply stage the changes you forgot, and use the `--amend` option with `git commit`. Let's illustrate with an example. First, we create a repository with a file named `file1.txt` which we commit:

<pre class="terminal">
$ mkdir ~/example01-undoing-changes
$ cd ~/example01-undoing-changes
$ git init
$ echo "Some contents" > file1.txt
$ git add file1.txt
$ git commit -m "Add file.txt"
$ git log --oneline
<span class="col-hash">1d38fb6</span> <span class="col-yellow">(</span><span class="col-head">HEAD</span> <span class="col-yellow">-></span> <span class="col-branch-local">main</span><span class="col-yellow">)</span> Add file.txt
</pre>

Now let's imagine we forgot to add some changes before making the commit. We also notice that we wrote `Add file.txt` not `Add file1.txt` in the commit message. We can amend the current commit by making the additional changes, add them to the staging area, and make another commit using the `--amend` option:

<pre class="terminal">
$ echo "More contents" >> file1.txt
$ git add file1.txt
$ git commit --amend -m "Add file1.txt"
$ git log --oneline
<span class="col-hash">32c7f65</span> <span class="col-yellow">(</span><span class="col-head">HEAD</span> <span class="col-yellow">-></span> <span class="col-branch-local">main</span><span class="col-yelloe">)</span> Add file1.txt
$ cat file1.txt
Some contents
More contents
</pre>

Notice how we still only have one commit in the repository, but the commit ID has changed, and the commit message has been updated.

It's important to understand that what Git is doing here is not so much "amending" the commit, but *replacing* it with a new commit that will have a new checksum, as also illustrated in the above example. Amending a commit is an example of rewriting the commit history of the Git repository. We will not go into more details on this at this point, but rewriting the commit history should be done with care if you are collaborating with other on a Git repository.


## Restoring the working tree and staging area

The `git restore` command can be used to restores files in the staging area and working directory with content from a restore source. We can use this command to undo changes we have made in the working tree, unstage changes from the staging area, and also restore earlier versions of files.


### Discarding changes in the working tree

Running `git restore <file>` without any options, restores `<file>` in the working tree using the content of the `<file>` in the current commit. That is to say, any unstaged changes in the working tree version of `<file>` are discarded. Let's illustrate this with an example. First, we create a repository with a commit of a file named `file1.txt`:

<pre class="terminal">
$ mkdir ~/example02-undoing-changes
$ cd ~/example02-undoing-changes
$ git init
$ echo "Contents of first commit" > file1.txt
$ git add file1.txt
$ git commit -m "Add file1.txt"
</pre>

Next, we make changes in the working tree but decide, that we do not want those changes anyway. We can use `git restore file1.txt` to discard them:

<pre class="terminal">
$ echo "Unstaged changes in working tree" >> file1.txt
$ cat file1.txt
Contents of first commit
Unstaged changes in working tree
$ git restore file1.txt
$ cat file1.txt
Contents of first commit
</pre>

After using `git restore file1.txt` the working tree version of `file1.txt` has been restore using the version of `file1.txt` from the current commit.

*Warning:* You need to be careful when using `git restore <file>`. You will discard any unstaged changes, and will not be able to recover them.


### Unstaging changes

We can unstage changes using `git restore --staged <file>`. This will restore the staging area with the staging area from the current commit, effectively unstaging changes you have staged. Let's illustrate this by continuing the previous example:

<pre class="terminal">
$ echo "Staged contents" >> file1.txt
$ git add file1.txt
$ git status
On branch main
Changes to be committed:
  (use "git restore --staged <file>..." to unstage)
<span class="col-status-staged">        modified:   file1.txt</span>

$ git restore --staged file1.txt
$ git status
On branch main
Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
<span class="col-status-not-staged">        modified:   file1.txt</span>

no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")
</pre>

What `git restore --staged file1.txt` has done here, is to restore the version of `file1.txt` in the staging area, with the version of `file1.txt` from the current commit.


### Restoring a previous version of a file

When not specified, the implicit restore source used by `git restore` is `HEAD`. We can explicitly specify it with the the `--source` option as `git restore --source=HEAD`. We can use the `--source` option to choose another restore source. Let's illustrate by continuing our example. Let's illustrate this with a new example. First, we create a repository with 3 commits of a file named `file1.txt`:

<pre class="terminal">
$ mkdir ~/example03-undoing-changes
$ cd ~example03-undoing-changes
$ echo "Contents in first commit" > file1.txt
$ git add file1.txt
$ git commit -m "First commit"
$ echo "Contents in second commit" > file2.txt
$ git add file1.txt
$ git commit -m "Second commit"
$ echo "Contents in third commit" > file3.txt
$ git add file1.txt
$ git commit -m "Third commit"
</pre>

We can restore the first version of `file1.txt` in the working tree, by identifying the first commit ID, and using the `--source` option with `git restore`:

<pre class="terminal">
$ git log --oneline
<span class="col-hash">85eef66</span> <span class="col-yellow">(</span><span class="col-head">HEAD</span> <span class="col-yellow">-></span> <span class="col-branch-local">main</span><span class="col-yellow">)</span> Third commit
<span class="col-hash">5fa3962</span> Second commit
<span class="col-hash">b9ab876</span> First commit
$ cat fil1.txt
Contents of third commit
$ git restore --source=b9ab876 file1.txt
$ cat file1.txt
Contents of first commit
$ git status
On branch main
Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
<span class="col-status-not-staged">        modified:   file1.txt</span>

no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")
</pre>

If we wanted to stage this change for the next commit we could use `git add`, but we could also restore the first version of `file1.txt` in the staging area using the `--staged` option:

<pre class="terminal">
$ git restore --staged --source=b9ab876 file1.txt
$ git status
On branch main
Changes to be committed:
  (use "git restore --staged <file>..." to unstage)
<span class="col-status-staged">        modified:   file1.txt</span>

</pre>

## Moving `HEAD` to undo commits

You can move `HEAD` to an earlier commit using `git reset`, and depending on the options we use, we can either preserve or discard the changes introduced by the subsequent commits. This effectively allows us to undo commits. Let's illustrate this with an example. First, we create a repository with two commits of a file named `file1.txt`:

<pre class="terminal">
$ mkdir ~/example04-undoing-changes
$ cd ~/example04-undoing-changes
$ git init
$ echo "Contents in first commit" > file1.txt
$ git add file1.txt
$ git commit -m "Add file1.txt"
$ echo "Contents added in second commit" >> file1.txt
$ git add file1.txt
$ git commit -m "Update file1.txt"
$ git log --oneline
32f2155 (HEAD -> main) Update file1.txt
0c68ac6 Add file1.txt
</pre>


<pre class="terminal">
$ git reset HEAD^
Unstaged changes after reset:
M       file1.txt
$ cat file1.txt
Contents in first commit
$ git log --oneline
0c68ac6 (HEAD -> main) Add file1.txt
$ git status
On branch main
Changes not staged for commit:
  (use "git add <file>..." to update what will be committed)
  (use "git restore <file>..." to discard changes in working directory)
        modified:   file1.txt

no changes added to commit (use "git add" and/or "git commit -a")
$ git diff
diff --git a/file1.txt b/file1.txt
index ce44375..bd77fb7 100644
--- a/file1.txt
+++ b/file1.txt
@@ -1 +1,2 @@
 Contents in first commit
+Contents added in second commit
$
</pre>

We can see that `HEAD` has been moved to the first commit, effectively undoing the second commit. We also see that the changes introduced in the second commmit are still staged.



## Summary

In this chapter, you learned how to undo changes and correct mistakes in a Git repository.

- `git commit --amend` allows you to modify the most recent commit, for example to correct its commit message or include additional changes.

- `git restore` allows you to discard changes in the working tree or unstage changes without discarding them. You can also use it to restore earlier versions of files.

- `git reset` allows you to move the current branch back to an earlier commit. Depending on the options used, you can either preserve or discard the changes introduced by subsequent commits.

Some of these operations can permanently discard changes, while others modify the commit history. You should therefore use them carefully, particularly when working with commits that have already been shared with others.


## Exercises


### Exercise 1 - Amending commits

In this exercise you will practice amending commits. Run the following commands to set up a repository with a single commit of a file named `file1.txt`:

<pre class="terminal">
$ mkdir ~/ex01-undoing-changes
$ cd ~/ex01-undoing-changes
$ git init
$ echo "Draft of contents" > file1.txt
$ git add file1.txt
$ git commit -m "Add file1.txt
</pre>

<b>1. Update `file1.txt` by amending the commit.</b>

Change the line in `file1.txt` from `Draft of contents` to `Contents`, stage the changes, and amend the changes to the existing commit. Keep the existing commit message. Run `git log --oneline` before and after amending the commit, and explain what has changed and why.

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" collapse="true" icon="false"}

<pre class="terminal">
$ echo "Contents" > file1.txt
$ git add file1.txt
$ git log --oneline
86b78d9 (HEAD -> main) Add file1.txt
$ git commit --amend -m "Add file1.txt"
$ git log --oneline
8d1a459 (HEAD -> main) Add file1.txt
</pre>

The commit ID of the commit has changed, because the commit has been amended, replacing the old commit with a new commit.

:::

<b>2. Reusing the commit message.</b>

Run the following commands to stage additional changes to `file1.txt` that we once again wish to amend to the first commit:

<pre class="terminal">
$ echo "More content" >> file1.txt
$ git add file1.txt
</pre>

In Step 1 we had to either use the `-m` option to specify the new commit message, or confirm the commit message in a text editor. When we are amending a commit but we do not wish to alter the commit message, this is inconvenient. Consult the `git commit` documentation to find an option that allows us use the existing commit message without launching a text editor, and use this option to amend the commit with the new changes.

::: {.callout-tip title="Hint 1" collapse="true" icon="false"}

The `git commit` documentation is extensive, including many options. Press `<Ctrl> + f` in your browser and search for `--amend` to see if the option we are looking for is described near the use of `--amend` in the documentation.

:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Hint 2" collapse="true" icon="false"}

The option we are looking for is `--no-edit`.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Solution" collapse="true" icon="false"}

<pre class="terminal">
$ git commit --amend --no-edit
</pre>

:::
